(9:15) Select Board Minutes Tuesday, September 29, 2026 7:00pm A regular meeting of the Select Board (the “Board”) of the Town of Harvard (the “Town”) was held virtually on Tuesday, September 29, 2026 in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain Covid-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. Select Board Participants: Ahmet Corapcioglu, Vice-Chair; Kara McGuire Minar; Eve Wittenberg; Eric Ward. Absent: SusanMary Redinger. Town Department Participants: Dawn Dunbar, Town Administrator; Julie Doucet, Assistant Town Administrator/Human Resources Director; Michelle Stockman, Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator. Additional Participants: Andres Correa, Energy Manager; Ellen Sachs Leicher, Harvard Climate Initiative Committee Chair and Harvard Energy Advisory Committee Member. A quorum was declared and the meeting was called to order by Vice-Chair Ahmet Corapcioglu at 7:00pm. Michelle Stockman kept the minutes of the meeting. The Vice-Chair opened the meeting to public communication, and there being no questions, comments, or concerns, proceeded to business matters. The upcoming Department of Public Works (“DPW”) information sessions, scheduled to be held on October 5 and October 8, were previewed. Prior Meeting Minutes Vice-Chair Corapcioglu asked whether the Board had any comments concerning the prior meeting minutes from September 1, 20261 and September 15, 20262 distributed and revised in advance of the meeting. There being no questions or concerns, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu declared them approved as revised. Appointments & Resignations In recognition of their service to the Agricultural Advisory Commission, the Board thanked Christiane Turnheim following their resignation on September 18, 2026.3 The Board also extended its gratitude to Rainer Park, who resigned from the Bare Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee on September 8, 2026.4 Next, a motion was made by Eve Wittenberg and seconded by Kara McGuire Minar to appoint Jo-Anne Crystoff, previously an alternate, as a regular member Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 1 of the Bare Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee.5 By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was then made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to re-appoint Jim Lee as the Harvard Conservation Trust’s representative on the Open Space Committee.6 By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Following their resignation on September 19, 2026, the Board thanked Seth Trotz for their service to the Warner Free Lecture Trustees.7 It was noted that, although this was an elected position, the Board was able to appoint someone to fill the vacancy until the next election. The Chair of the Warner Free Lecture Trustees was working to identify such a candidate. For those interested in volunteering, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu highlighted the board and committee vacancies available, which could be viewed on the Town’s website. Amendment to One-Day License: Harvard Alpaca Ranch A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to amend the Harvard Alpaca Ranch’s one-day liquor license, changing the event date from September 26 to October 11, due to inclement weather.8 By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Energy Manager Report At the invitation of the Board, Energy Manager Andres Correa presented a year-one report on his work across four towns: Groton, Harvard, Ayer, and Shirley.9 The position was funded by a Mass Save Municipal Energy Management Grant, sponsored by National Grid, for which the four towns applied jointly with support from the school district, Groton Sustainability Commission, and Harvard Climate Initiative Committee. Mr. Correa highlighted grant awards totaling $734,851 in funding and an estimated annual savings of $60,286. Harvard, specifically, was awarded a $201,851 grant to fund the library’s heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (“HVAC”) system’s coil retrofit and replacement of equipment. The Board and Harvard Climate Initiative Committee Chair Ellen Sachs Leicher commended Mr. Correa on his strong contributions. They also expressed interest in continuing the position beyond the current three-year period. Local Action Unit Application for Emerson Green Project Speaking on behalf of the Municipal Affordable Housing Trust, Ms. Wittenberg provided an update on the Emerson Green affordable housing project, explaining that twelve units would be designated as local action units (each, an “LAU”) at 80% area median income, representing 25% of the total number of units in the development and helping the Town meet its affordable housing goals. Ms. Wittenberg summarized the Town’s application to the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (the “EOHLC”), which required the Board’s approval and signature.10 If the application was approved and the units deemed compliant, all 46 units would be included in the Town’s subsidized housing inventory and available to qualifying residents. A discussion ensued regarding the housing production timeline and plan. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to approve the Town’s LAU application to the EOHLC, and that the Chair or Vice-Chair of the Board be authorized to sign it. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Finalization of Special Town Meeting Warrant Vice-Chair Corapcioglu invited comments on the nine articles of the Special Town Meeting warrant (the “warrant”), distributed in advance of the meeting.11 There were no questions or concerns. It was noted that the Finance Committee would submit its recommendations separately. A motion was made by Ms. Minar Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 2 and seconded by Mr. Ward to close the warrant. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. The Board then proceeded to review and vote upon recommendations for each warrant article in turn. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 1 to pay bills of prior fiscal years. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Mr. Ward to recommend Article 2 regarding the payment of $14,934 to cover the school ESSER grant deficit. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 3 to approve the Capital Planning and Investment Committee’s recommended expenditure for the acquisition of a police cruiser and water meters. It was clarified that the proposed police cruiser was a hybrid vehicle. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 4 to amend Chapter 78 of the Town’s code, as proposed by the Personnel Board. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 5 to replace Section 125-53 of the Town’s Bylaws with a new Clean Energy Facilities bylaw, as proposed by the Planning Board with consideration of resident feedback. It was clarified that this would align the Town’s solar bylaws with new State regulations. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 6 to amend Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws to conform with Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 40A as proposed by the Planning Board. Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar confirmed that the Planning Board had closed its hearing the previous night and that Town counsel had reviewed the final draft. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 7 to reorganize Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws pertaining to use regulations, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 40. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 8 to reorganize Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws pertaining to dimensional regulations, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 9 to revise Section 125-60 of the Town’s Bylaws regarding the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority Communities Multi-Family Overlay District, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 3 Before proceeding, the Board discussed next steps, which included preparing the motions and assigning responsibilities for the Special Town Meeting on October 20. Fiscal Year 2028 (“FY28”) Budget Guidance Eric Ward led the Board in a review of a draft memorandum (“memo”) outlining the FY28 budget guidance discussed at the September 22 meeting. The memo outlined the budget target and standards, submission guidelines, and revenue opportunities. Budget proposals would be due to the Board by November 30. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to approve and distribute the FY28 budget guidance. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Position Letter re: H.5175/S.3166 Vice-Chair Corapcioglu presented a letter to Senator James Eldridge and Representative Danillo Sena concerning the Energy Affordability Conference Committee’s reconciliation of H.5175 and S.3166.12 The letter supported the Legislature’s goals of reducing energy costs and decarbonizing buildings, and asked that the final bill preserve municipal authority in implementing clean-energy policy, including protections for Mass Save funding and competitive energy supplier contracts. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Mr. Ward to approve the position letter as written and authorize either the Chair or Vice-Chair of the Board to sign it. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. All Boards Meeting Scheduling The Board addressed scheduling challenges and considered several dates for the upcoming Select Board and All Boards meetings due to conflicts with the Special Town Meeting, State election, and Veterans Day. The Board deferred the decision to its next meeting. Town Administrator Report (Attachment A) At the invitation of the Board, Ms. Dunbar delivered a Town Administrator Report. Project updates included: a pre-construction meeting on October 5 regarding the Ayer Road Transportation Improvement Program project; and the addition of a firebox to bring the Harvard/Devens Water System Interconnection Pump Station into compliance with safety requirements. With respect to personnel, Ms. Dunbar announced that Colin Hayes had been hired as an Equipment Operator/Mechanic for the DPW, effective September 29. Ms. Dunbar then reported on weekly meetings with NextGen, the Shirley Town Administrator, and the Ayer Town Manager, regarding the re-scoped budget for a $1M Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness Action Grant. Select Board Reports Mr. Ward noted upcoming Personnel Board meetings to discuss the annual cost-of-living adjustment. He reported that the School Committee was re-examining elements of the HVAC project while the Charter Review Committee continued its review work. Ms. Wittenberg reported on behalf of the Municipal Affordable Housing Trust, Conservation Commission, Open Space Committee, Tree Warden, and Agricultural Advisory Commission. The Affordable Housing Trust’s highlights included: a Habitat for Humanity Critical Repair Program information session to be held on October 13 in collaboration with the Council on Aging; and a housing development project awarded by MassDevelopment to Metro West Collaborative Developers for 65 affordable units at Adams Circle. The Conservation Commission planned to discuss the annual Bare Hill Pond drawdown further before making its Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 4 decision. The Tree Warden was developing a memorandum of understanding with the schools regarding responsibility for trees on school property. Ms. Wittenberg highlighted the Agricultural Advisory Commission’s need for new members. Ms. Minar reported that the Town Common flag, damaged in the recent storm, needed to be replaced. She also noted that funding for the Fivesparks grant through Senator Eldridge’s office remained pending due to unresolved budget matters. On behalf of the Park and Recreation Committee, Ms. Minar updated the Board on plans to reseed the field at Harvard Park. On behalf of the Community Media Access Committee, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu reported a successful open house following an expedited inspection of the new Harvard Media Cooperative production studio located at the school. Public Communication The meeting was opened to public communication. There being no questions, comments, or concerns, the Board briefly previewed the next meeting’s agenda. Announcements/No ﬁca ons/Mail/Other:  None 1 Select Board Minutes Tuesday, October 6, 2026 7:00pm A regular meeting of the Select Board (the “Board”) of the Town of Harvard (the “Town”) was held virtually on Tuesday, October 6, 2026 in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain Covid-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. Select Board Participants: SusanMary Redinger, Chair; Ahmet Corapcioglu, Vice-Chair; Kara McGuire Minar; Eve Wittenberg; Eric Ward. Town Department Participants: Dawn Dunbar, Town Administrator; Julie Doucet, Assistant Town Administrator/Human Resources Director; Michelle Stockman, Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator. Not to reconvene in open session. Vil. ADJOURNMENT Rules of Procedure for Board Meetings of Lanesborough Select Board Meetings L IL. A. B. AGENDA The Town Administrative Assistant, in consultation with the Town Administrator and Chairman of the Select Board shall prepare an Agenda for the Select Board meetings. Any requests for matters to be placed on the agenda shall be submitted in writing to the Town Administrative Assistant by noon three business days prior to regularly scheduled meetings. Anyone requesting items be placed on the agenda shall provide the topic of the item and sufficient information and detail so as to provide a reasonable notice of the nature and purpose of the agenda item. Agendas will be posted a minimum of 48 hours in advance of any meeting on our Town website and Town bulletin board. Those wishing to speak in the public comment portion of the agenda shall provide their name and the topic of their comment. Topics shall be limited to matters of concem, official action or deliberation which are or may be before the Select Board. MEETINGS Public Notice of the meetings shall be advertised and posted by the Administrative Assistant as required by law. The Chairman of the Select Board shall direct the meeting. In the absence of the Chairman, the senior member of the Select Board shall direct the meeting and shall have all powers and duties of the Chairman. Ow > The Modern Rules of Order shall be used to conduct the meeting unless otherwise modified by these Rules or altered by the Select Board. The Lanesborough Select Board shall be addressed by their respective titles. Residents and/or taxpayers may use audio or stenographic recorders to record all or any portion of the meeting. Said recorders shall be operated froin the area set aside for the general public seating and may not be placed on the Select Board’s table without prior consent of the Chairman. © Video recorders may be used to record all or any portion of a public meeting. The operator of the recorder shall remain seated in the area set aside for the general public or stand in the rear or to the side of the general public seating area so as to not interfere in any way with the activities of the Select Board or the ability of the general public to observe the Board. PUBLIC COMMENT Residents and taxpayers of Lanesborough shall have the right to speak in the meetings during the Public Comment portion of the agenda. In order to conduct meetings in an orderly and productive manner the following rules and regulations shall govern such speakers: Comment from residents/taxpayers shall be received only after the speaker is recognized by the Chairman. The speaker shall announce his or her name and address prior to addressing the Select Board. The Chairman may rule out-of-order scandalous, impertinent, irrelevant, and redundant comments, or comments that attempt to disrupt or needlessly protract the proceedings of the meeting. The Chairman may request any individual to leave the meeting and may contact security to that end when that individual does not observe reasonable decorum. Further, the Chairman may request the assistance of law enforcement officers to remove a disorderly person when his/her conduct interferes with the orderly progress of the meeting. The Chairman may call a recess or adjournment to another time when the lack of public decorum interferes with the orderly conduct of the meeting. The Chairman may allocate available time among individuals wishing to comment. Time allocated for the public comment period at each meeting shall not exceed thirty (30) minutes and limited to citizens of Lanesborough unless prior approval is granted by the Lanesborough Select Board. Each speaker will be allotted three (3) minutes to present his or her topic. Said time limitations may be altered or waived at the Chairman’s direction. At the discretion of the Chairman conducting the meeting, a group of citizens registered to address the Select Board on the same issue may be required to designate a spokesperson.

Oleskiewicz 69 Main Street #202 North Adams, MA 01247 By Tina Marie Leonesio Date:11/3/2026 EMAIL Time: 11:59 AM November 1, 2026 Dear Honorable Members of the City Council: I am writing to respectfully express my interest in being considered for appointment to the vacant seat on the North Adams City Council. As you know, I previously had the privilege of serving on the City Council for five years, having initially been appointed through the convention process. During my tenure, I served on several committees, including Public Services, Public Safety, and General Government. These experiences gave me valuable insight into our city's operations, the challenges we face, and the importance of thoughtful decision-making, collaboration, and responsible leadership. My commitment to public service has continued beyond my time on the Council. I currently serve on the Hoosac Water Quality District and the North Adams Planning Board, where I remain actively involved in matters that directly impact our community and its future. As a lifelong resident of North Adams, I care deeply about our city, its residents, and its continued success. North Adams is my home, and I take great pride in being part of this community. I have always believed that public service is about more than attending meetings and making decisions. It is about listening to people, understanding their concerns, working together to find solutions, and making a positive difference in the lives of those we represent. I truly miss being part of the City Council and having the opportunity to contribute directly to the progress of our city. Most importantly, I miss the opportunity to help people and be a voice for the residents of North Adams. I believe my previous Council experience, continued involvement in city government, and genuine dedication to our community would allow me to step into this role and make an immediate, meaningful contribution. I would be honored to serve the residents of North Adams once again and respectfully ask for your consideration and support in filling this vacancy. Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued service to our city. Respectfully submitted, Peter J. RECEIVED AT CITY CLERK'S OFFICE By Tina Marie Leonesio Date: Time: City of North Adams In City Council POSTED: November 4, 2026 Council Order Number: 12,572 X November 04, 2026 4:30 PM An Ordinance to Amend the Revised Ordinances of the City of North Adams, Chapter 21 Streets and Sidewalks, Sections 21-25, 21-25.1 and 21-25.2 for Wheeled Vehicle use on Public Ways. In City Council on October 27, 2026 A Motion by Councilor Lisa Blackmer, seconded by Councilor Bryan Sapienza, VOTED by Yea/Nay vote to Pass to a Second Reading and Publish as a Municipal Bulletin as required by Law. (9) Yea’s; Councilors Blackmer, Bona, Breen, Fitch, MacDonald, McCarron, Sapienza, Shade, and Zavatsky; (0) Nays; (0) Abstain. Attest, Ashley Shade, President City Council Tina Marie Leonesio, City Clerk PLEASE DO NOT REMOVE POSTING If you would like a copy, PLEASE SEE: Tina Marie Leonesio, City Clerk City of North Adams In City Council ___ ___ Ordained: Date: November 10, 2026 BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of North Adams as follows: An Ordinance to amend the Ordinance Chapter 21, Sections 21-25 entitled “Bicycle riding roller skating, in-line skating and skateboarding on sidewalks” Section 21-25.1 entitled “Roller skating, in-line skating and skateboarding in the Business District. Section 21-25.2 entitled “Shopping Carts” Delete Sections 21-25, 21-25.1, and 21.25.2 in their entirety and replace with the following: Sec. 21-25. Wheeled vehicle riding or use on sidewalks or public rights of way. 21-25.1.0. Definitions a.) Wheeled vehicle – A vehicle of pleasure, burden, or transportation, self powered or manually powered, equipped with wheels, not classified as motor vehicle in MGL. b.) Mobility Vehicle – A transportation device used by individuals with disabilities to gain or assist with mobility as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act. c.) Electric bicycle, a bicycle or tricycle equipped with fully operable pedals and an electric motor, capable of speeds in excess of 20MPH. Specific classes of electric bicycles are described in Section 21-25.1.0.c.1 through 21-25.1.0.c.3. 1.) Class 1 Electric bicycle, an electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that provides assistance only when the rider is pedaling and that ceases to 1|Page City of North Adams In City Council provide assistance when the bicycle reaches the speed of 20 miles per hour. In accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1 “Definitions” 2.) Class 2 electric bicycle, an electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that may be used exclusively to propel the bicycle and that is not capable of providing assistance when the bicycle reaches the speed of 20 miles per hour, in accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1 “Definitions” 3.) Unclassified Electric Bicycle Exceeding Class 1 or Class 2 – any electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that is capable of speeds in excess of 28MPH. d.) Motorized scooter'', any 2 wheeled tandem or 3 wheeled device, that has handlebars, designed to be stood or sat upon by the operator, powered by an electric or gas powered motor that is capable of propelling the device with or without human propulsion. The definition of ''motorized scooter'' shall not include a motorcycle, electric bicycle or motorized bicycle or a 3 wheeled motorized wheelchair. e.) Public Thoroughfare – Any Publicly owned way or path that allows public passage. This includes streets and roads, walking paths, sidewalks, or other public right-of-ways. f.) Shared-Use Path or Trail – A public thoroughfare primarily designed for use by both pedestrians and bicycles. 21-25.1.1. Prohibition of vehicles on Sidewalks No person shall drive, wheel, or propel, any wheeled vehicle of pleasure upon or along any sidewalk or prohibited public right of way, except for the purpose of crossing such sidewalk or right of way to access property or buildings. If any such vehicle must be transported along a sidewalk to access the road or other area, it must be dismounted and pushed or carried by hand to such location as necessary and not ridden in any way. This prohibition does not apply to vehicles, exempted in Section 21-25.1.2. 2|Page City of North Adams In City Council 21-25.1.2 Exemptions to prohibition of vehicles on sidewalks The prohibitions of Section 21-25.1.1 do not apply to mobility vehicles, strollers and carriages, or hand powered vehicles of burden, such as wagons, personal shopping carts, or any other hand powered vehicle designed to carry goods or materials. Nor does this section apply to police officers or public safety officials on bicycles when engaged in the lawful performance of their duties. 21-25.1.3. Prohibition of wheeled vehicles on public thoroughfares during special events. No person shall drive, wheel, or propel any wheeled vehicle during designated special events, on public ways closed off to normal traffic or any other right of way when it is closed off to normal traffic for purposes of demonstrations or shows, unless such vehicle is part of the demonstration. If any vehicle that is not part of the event, must be transported through such a designated area, it must be dismounted, pushed, or carried through the area. This prohibition does not apply to exempted vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2. 21-25.1.4 Operation of wheeled vehicles on public roadways. Operation of wheeled vehicles on public road ways shall be in accordance with all state and local traffic ordinances. This includes the observance of traffic signs, signals, and pavement markings. 21-25.1.5 Operation of wheeled vehicles in crosswalks. No person shall ride any wheeled vehicle through a crosswalk. If it is necessary to use a crosswalk with such vehicles, the vehicle must be dis-mounted and pushed by hand through the 3|Page City of North Adams In City Council crosswalk. Wheeled vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2 are exempt from the prohibitions in this section and are considered the same as pedestrians. 21-25.1.6 Operation of wheeled vehicles on pedestrian bridges. No person shall ride any wheeled vehicle on any bridge for pedestrian use except wheeled vehicles exempted in Section 21-25.1.2. If a wheeled vehicle must use a pedestrian bridge, it must be dismounted and propelled by hand across the bridge. Pedestrians shall have the right of way, on any such bridge. 21-25.1.7 Use of Motorized vehicles on shared-use paths or trails. No motorized vehicles may be used on shared-use paths or trails, with the exception of Class 1 electric bicycles and motorized mobility vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2, unless otherwise posted. Speed of any vehicle on such trails or paths shall not exceed 15MPH. 21-25.1.8. Helmets, use of MGL Chapter 85, Section 11B1/2 Requires any person 16 years of age or younger operating in line skates, a skate board, a scooter or other manually-propelled wheeled vehicle or riding as a passenger on any such manually-propelled vehicle on a public way, bicycle path or on any other public right-of-way shall wear a helmet. Such helmet shall fit the person's head and be secured by straps at all times while operating in line skates, scooters, skate board or other manually-propelled wheeled vehicle and shall meet the standards for helmets established by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI Z 90.4) or subsequent standards or the Snell Memorial Foundation's 1984 standard for use in bicycling or subsequent standards. A violation of this section shall not be used as evidence of contributory negligence in a civil action. a). Helmets are required by persons of all ages while riding a vehicle described in 4|Page City of North Adams In City Council Section 21-25.1.0.a while riding on any public thoroughfare in the City of North Adams. This shall include passengers on any such vehicle designed to carry a passenger. 21-25.1.9. Prohibition of wheeled vehicles where posted. Operation of wheeled vehicles shall be prohibited, where posted by sign or ordinance. 21-25.1.10. Safe use of wheeled vehicles on public thoroughfares. Operation of all wheeled vehicles shall be in accordance with applicable MGL and local ordinances. This includes whether or not the vehicle is designed to carry a passenger. 21-25.1.11 Unsafe operation of wheeled vehicles. Persons observed to be operating any wheeled vehicle in an unsafe manner, or to be found in violation of this section, shall be issued a citation and may be subject to penalties as described in Section 21-25.1.11. MGL Chapter 85, Section 11e permits the citation to be issued to the parent or guardian of the operator, if the operator of such vehicle is under age 18. 21-25.1.12 Penalties Violators of this section shall be subject to one or more of the following penalties: a.) Fines in accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1e as stated in Appendix D-8. b.) Confiscation of vehicle for a period of no less than 24 hours nor greater than 48 hours from the time of the infraction. 21-25.2. Shopping Carts 5|Page City of North Adams In City Council Store owned shopping carts are not permitted on any street, sidewalk, or public right of way and shall not be removed from the cart owner's property. This prohibition does not apply to personally owned shopping carts used to transport goods from store to home. This prohibition does not apply to personally owned baskets or carts attached to mobility vehicles. 21-25.2.1. Removal of shopping carts from sidewalks. Owners of commercial shopping carts must remove and retrieve shopping carts from public sidewalks or other public rights of way within 24 hours of a complaint by police or citizen reporting such abandoned carts. Carts not picked up by the owner shall be removed by the Public Works Department and disposed of accordingly. The Public Works Department shall not be responsible for returning said carts to store owners. 6|Page Date: ___October 27, 2026___ BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of North Adams as follows: Chapter 2.22 Remove “Reserved”. Insert Title as 2.22: North Adams Safeguards for Artificial Intelligence, Fairness & Equity (S.A.F.E. AI) Insert Sections in full as follows: SECTION 2.22.1. AUTHORITY AND SHORT TITLE This Ordinance shall be known and may be cited as the “NA S.A.F.E. AI Ordinance,” which stands for “North Adams Safeguards for Artificial Intelligence, Fairness & Equity Ordinance.” This Ordinance governs the municipal acquisition, deployment, and use of Artificial Intelligence systems by the City of North Adams and its departments. SECTION 2.22.2. PURPOSE, FINDINGS, AND CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS The City Council finds that Artificial Intelligence technologies are rapidly transforming government operations, local economies, and civic life. Municipal adoption of AI must safeguard constitutional rights, civil liberties, and equal protection under the law. The purpose of this Ordinance is to establish safeguards governing municipal AI use; protect civil liberties, due process, privacy, and equal protection; prevent unlawful discrimination and automated harm; promote transparency and democratic accountability; ensure responsible innovation that strengthens the City of North Adams; and align municipal AI governance with constitutional principles and ethical public administration. The City affirms that technological efficiency shall not supersede individual dignity. SECTION 2.22.3. DEFINITIONS AI Audit: A documented review of a High-Risk AI System’s operation, accuracy, reliability, disparate impact, human overrides, data practices, security controls, compliance with this Ordinance, and material changes since the prior review. Algorithmic Impact Assessment: A documented evaluation of a proposed AI System that identifies its intended purpose, affected populations, data sources, decision-making role, foreseeable risks, accuracy and reliability concerns, potential discriminatory or disparate impacts, privacy and security risks, human oversight mechanisms, vendor obligations, and available mitigation measures. 1 | Page Anonymized Data: Data altered through removal or transformation of identifying information so that the data cannot reasonably be used, alone or in combination with other reasonably available information, to identify a specific individual. Articulable Suspicion: Specific and objective facts, together with reasonable inferences from those facts, that provide an individualized basis for investigative or enforcement attention. Artificial Intelligence System (AI System): A machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, processes data using machine learning, statistical modeling, generative techniques, or comparable computational methods to produce predictions, classifications, recommendations, content, or decisions that materially assist municipal operations or decision-making. Automated Decision System (ADS): An AI System used to materially assist or replace discretionary decision-making that affects legal rights, benefits, employment, public safety enforcement, housing, permitting, licensing, or access to City services. City Data: Information collected, created, received, maintained, purchased, licensed, or otherwise possessed by or on behalf of the City in connection with municipal operations, excluding information lawfully obtained by a Vendor independently of its work for the City. Civil Rights and Equity Impact Assessment: A documented evaluation conducted before deployment of a High-Risk AI System that examines whether the system may create or contribute to unlawful discrimination, disparate impact, unequal treatment, or impairment of civil rights or civil liberties, and identifies measures necessary to prevent, reduce, or remedy such risks. Continuous Indiscriminate Tracking: Ongoing or repeated monitoring of an individual’s location, movement, activities, or associations without an individualized investigative or other lawful basis. External Entity Access: The ability of any person, business, contractor, vendor, nonprofit organization, governmental entity, or other third party outside the government of the City of North Adams to view, search, retrieve, receive, obtain, or otherwise access City Data or data generated through a Cityoperated or City-contracted AI System. Generalized Behavioral Aggregation: The collection or combination of data concerning an individual’s activities, movements, associations, communications, or behavior for the purpose of creating a behavioral profile unrelated to a specific lawful investigation or municipal function. 2 | Page High-Risk AI System: An AI System used to Materially Influence decisions that: 1. Affect an individual’s legal rights, benefits, or access to public services; 2. Impact employment

Rebecca Brien, Pittsfield, is in support of a 10-rninute loading zone sign in front of That's a Wrap Cafe. Luke Pryjrna, Gt. Barrington, commented about DEi and comments from the last council meeting, stating DEi is a small economic portion of the city budget. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. COMMUNICATIONS FROM HIS HONOR THE MAYOR A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to accept a grant funds in the amount of $10,500.00 from the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection. Councilor Conant made a motion to accept the grant carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to pay a previous year's expense in the amount of $2,083.06 from FY27 Parking expense account. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vole of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $5,417.82 between line items within the FY27 Building Inspectors Budget. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve, carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $67,504.00 from Public Works· Sewer Enterprise salary accounts to the Public Works Sewer Enterprise expense account. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve. Councilor Kavey asked Commissioner Morales to explain what happened with the two positions. The Commissioner stated these are multiple positions, the chief TPO is one position, and the head TPO has multiple staff. They had vacancies and transitions in leadership for two or three months and some have just been filled. Councilor Cunningham asked what the contractual services this will be used for. The Commissioner stated it is for service from a consultant and a series of related things to new management, safety, operational training, that they are outsourcing for training purposes. Councilor Cunningham asked if this has anything to do with the lab. The Commissioner said one of the services will look at the processes in the lab but not the space. Councilor Moody asked the Commissioner about open spots taken out of the budget during budget season in which the mayor said when negotiations are finished with the union he will return to ask for more money when positions are filled. She has concerns moving the funding from a salary account to an expense account. The Commissioner stated that the enterprise was not in that discussion, these employees are roped in to the compensation study, not part of the positions that were not funded. Councilor Moody asked about the $300,000.00 allocated towards consulting services. The Commissioner stated that we have ongoing services related to our permit. This is different than this. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $200,000.00 from the Public Works Stabilization Fund for the purchase of equipment for the Department of Public Services. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve. Councilor Lampiasi asked the Commissioner about the timeline. Commissioner Morales stated that the equipment is necessary for a supervisor to go on the mains with a wing plow and to pick up that wing to go on a regular plow to go through the neighborhood streets. They have a vehicle that they have identified that can be expediated, so they do not have to wait the 10-12 months. Councilor Costa asked if this is going to increase our capacity to increase snow plowing. The Commissioner said it will. Councilor Cunningham asked if we have more plows than drivers. The Commissioner stated we have two plows like this currently that are spread out through the department. We have seven snow fighters, pickup trucks with plows, we do not have a plow truck with a wing and spreader capable of going on mains and neighborhoods. Councilor Warren suggested bringing things forward sooner and to inform the council when new equipment is necessary. The Commissioner stated he will communicate items like this in the future. Councilor White asked what type of truck will be purchased and can it be interchangeable. The Commissioner stated it is a one-ton pickup truck with attachments, plow, wing, and spreader. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. REPORTS FROM COMMITTEES Reports from the Public Health and Safety Committee A report from the Public Health and Safety Committee on a petition from Councilor White requesting an update from the EPA, DEP, and DPH concerning Building 71 and Hill 78, recommending to accept the report 4/0. Councilor Conant made a motion to accept the report and place on file. Councilor Warren asked Councilor Costa why the discussion did not touch on the public health component. Councilor Costa said this is an old petition. Councilor Costa stated that Richard Fisher from DPA gave an extensive presentation and answered many questions about the concerns for these areas. A follow-up question concerning storm water run off on Tyler Street Extension will be investigated. Councilor Moody is in communication with Mr. Fisher on this. Councilor Costa said there are plans to demolish the building 19 area and GE stated they have no plans to use the remaining buildings raised in that area for any purpose. They are considering a combination of fencing, plantings and grass with the final design not yet complete. The motion to accept and place on file carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. KOCH CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-148 ORDERED: November 09, 2026 BE IT ORDAINED that $4,170,000 (Four Million One Hundred Seventy Thousand Dollars) be appropriated for the purpose of financing the Phase 14 engineering and construction of sewer system improvement to remove Infiltration and Inflow (I/I) from the City’s sanitary sewer system, including the payment of costs incidental or related thereto. In order to meet this appropriation, the Treasurer-Collector with the approval of the Mayor is authorized to borrow $4,170,000 and to issue bonds and notes therefor under G.L. c.44, §§ 7(1) and/or 8(14), or any other enabling authority.. It is anticipated that this amount will be financed in whole or in part through the Massachusetts Water Resource Authority’s (MWRA) I/I Local Financial Assistance Program. The Treasurer-Collector and any other appropriate City official, with the approval of the Mayor, is authorized to borrow all or a portion of the $4,170,000 from the MWRA, or any source to fund this appropriation. The Treasurer-Collector is hereby authorized to enter into a loan agreement and/or security agreement with the MWRA relative to such loan, and the Commissioner of Public Works and any other appropriate City official, with the approval of the Mayor, is authorized to contract for and expend any Federal, State, or other aid available for the project, including any grant related to such program from the MWRA, and to take any other action necessary or convenient to carry out this project. INTRODUCED BY: WARD FOUR COUNCILLOR – VIRGINIA M. RYAN WARD ONE COUNCILLOR – DAVID A. JACOBS WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. RILEY COUNCILLOR AT LARGE – ZIQIANG SUSAN YUAN CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-150 ORDERED: November 09, 2026 R ESOLUTION OPPOSING EFFORTS TO WAIVE STATE CONSUMERPROTECTION LAWS FOR A LONG-TERM LEASE OF QUINCY’S BIGGEST PARCEL OF PUBLICLY OWNED OPEN SPACE WHEREAS, Quarry Hills Associates (QHA) currently holds a long-term lease with the City of Quincy for approximately 240 acres of municipal property operating as the Granite Links Golf Club; and WHEREAS, the current lease agreement has 30 years remaining in its term; and WHEREAS, state law limits the lease of public land to 30 years (MGL Chapter 40 section 3) and requires leases of public land to be put out to bid (MGL Chapter 30B section 16); and WHEREAS, the mayor and previous council sent a home-rule petition to state legislators asking for these requirements to be waived so that Quarry Hills Associates could sign a new lease for an additional 50 years, ending in 2106; and WHEREAS, Quincy’s state senator paused action on the petition in the Senate over uncertainty about whether the deal was in the best interests of Quincy taxpayers, requesting a formal audit (as requested by the City Council) and analyses of the proposed lease’s cost and hospitality terms; and WHEREAS, the House then inserted the petition’s language in a package of budget amendments that it passed, circumventing the home-rule petition’s deliberative process; and WHEREAS, that leaves the long-term fate of Quincy’s largest single piece of publicly owned open space subject to a back-room process where budget amendments are traded like baseball cards; and WHEREAS, deep concerns have been raised by citizen advocates, fiscal watchdogs, and state legislators regarding the lack of research on the terms of the current and proposed leases and the implications of future construction at the site; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 150 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, residents have expressed ongoing concerns regarding public access to the land, promised trail connections to the Blue Hills Reservation, traffic, and maintenance of the site’s athletic fields; and WHEREAS, entering a commitment that binds the City of Quincy and its taxpayers through the next century requires the highest threshold of community engagement, independent financial auditing, and due diligence to ensure maximum public benefit; NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council formally opposes any attempt to waive state laws that protect residents by limiting the lengths of leases of public land and by requiring open bids for leases of public land; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council urges the Massachusetts General Court to reject any consolidated budget amendments, home-rule petition, or other legislative maneuver that seeks to authorize this new lease without a comprehensive, independent fiscal analysis in the form of an audit and studies of cost and hospitality terms; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council requests that the Mayor’s administration halt lease negotiations and perform the requested financial accountability and due diligence to ensure that Quincy taxpayers get the most from any revenue-sharing formula; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that any proposed change to the current lease be returned to the Quincy City Council for discussion and oversight; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be sent to Quincy’s state legislative delegation, the Senate president, the chairs of the House and Senate Ways and Means Committees, the Governor, and the Lieutenant Governor. INTRODUCED BY: WARD THREE COUNCILLOR – WALTER HUBLEY WARD TWO COUNCILLOR – RICHARD C. ASH WARD FOUR COUNCILLOR – VIRGINIA M. RYAN WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. title: Planning Board Agenda and Items
text: Page 1 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 SEEKONK PLANNING BOARD Public Hearing, Regular Business, and Work Session Meeting Select Board Meeting Room October 27, 2026 Present: D. Sullivan, M. Bingham, P. Dunn, J. Perry, S. Smith, B. Hoch, and John Aubin (Town Planner) Absent with cause: S. Escaler Chair D. Sullivan opened the meeting at 7:02 PM Public Hearing: 1. Proposed amendments to the Zoning By-laws of the Town of Seekonk to Section 4.2.2 Institutional, Utility, and Recreational Uses. M. Bingham made a motion to open the public hearing. Seconded by B. Hoch. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, J. Perry: Recused herself from the public hearing, B. Hoch: AYE. P. Dunn made a motion to waive the reading of the public notice. Seconded by M. Bingham. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, B. Hoch: AYE. J. Aubin stated this is a petition received by the Town clerk that was then forwarded to the Select Board. This is the Planning Board’s public hearing on it and the Board will be making a report to Town Meeting. He was contacted by Christopher Rizzo to make a presentation. His understanding is that there will be a floor amendment proposed. This will be a question for the Town Moderator. The Planning Board is free to make a positive, negative, or no recommendation. Christopher Rizzo, of 305 Pleasant Street, made a presentation on the proposed amendments and gave a copy of that presentation to each Board member. Presentation entered into the record as attachment #1. C. Rizzo explained that due to deadlines for submittal, the original proposed language was overly complex. The language has since been simplified so that a floor amendment would be more easily digested. C. Rizzo further explained his research and reasoning for putting forth this amendment. D. Sullivan asked the Board if they had any questions for the applicant. D. Sullivan asked if there was anyone present to speak in favor the proposed amendments. John Alves, of 25 River Street, stated that he was on the Community Preservation Committee when the Medeiros Farm was purchased and passed at Town Meeting. He said that the purpose of the project was stated from the beginning. He stated that he hopes the Planning Board speaks in favor of this. Page 2 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 Anne Miller, of 25 River Stret, wanted to make a comment on the presentation. There is a standard process for municipal projects and if there is going to be a Zoning Board review, the final design is brought forward so the Zoning board can make informed decisions. She is in favor of this amendment because she believes it eliminated any confusion about process and allows projects to move forward with less hoops while still providing adequate review. Jean Stocker, of 14 Washington Street, stated that she sees this proposed amendment as following what is already being done in the State. She believes that anything that can help make things less contentious is a good thing. She believes the process is very convoluted right now. C. Rizzo said he wanted to reenforce that this only talks about the principal use table. Anything else with zoning bylaws, still falls under the existing processes. D. Sullivan asked if there was anyone who wanted to speak in opposition of the proposed amendments. Ken Kazarian, of 12 Kenwood Court, wanted to speak. He asked the Chair if he knew how many municipalities are in Massachusetts. D. Sullivan answered 351. K. Kazarian made a point that C. Rizzo only mentioned 10 in his presentation. He then stated he felt this is a contentious discussion amongst residents because there are people who live 30 feet from the proposed active recreation field. K. Kazarian said he is concerned about the long-term maintenance plan to keep up with the fields and believes that the town will rent out the fields to help offset the cost. He stated that he is not against the project, but he would like there to be consideration or the neighbor who want to come home on the weekend and enjoy their own backyard. He believes this kind of project does not belong in the middle of a residential neighborhood but rather next to a school. D. Sullivan reminded everyone that the discussion tonight is strictly in regards to the proposed Zoning by-law language and not to details of the Mederios Farm project. Cynthia Ward, of 6 Kenwood Court, wanted to read a letter and submit it into the public record. This letter has been entered into the record as attachment #2. C. Ward said she is an abutter to the proposed project. She said she has greater concerns than just in relation to the Mederios Farm. She then read her letter to the Planning Board. Her letter ended with five requests. J. Aubin reminded the Board that they are here to make a recommendation to the Select Board on the proposed Zoning amendment that was submitted by petition. This is not something that the Planning Board came up with, but rather a petition submitted to the Town Clerk that the Planning Board is now reviewing. B. Hoch needed clarification on the proposal. The proposal would remove the 2/3 vote requirement and thus make municipal uses allowed by right. C. Ward had a question related to the process. She asked if the neighbors respond to the submitted proposal, how could a change be brought up after? J. Aubin said a change to the proposed language could only happen on the floor at Town Meeting and would ultimately be allowed by the Town Moderator. S. Smith made a motion to close the public hearing. Seconded by M. Bingham. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, B. Hoch: AYE. D. Sullivan said he believes the Board can only act on what was presented in the packet and certified by the Town Clerk. Page 3 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 J. Aubin said the Planning Board can still take note of the testimony offered tonight and the statements made with regard to a floor amendment. Until the floor amendment is made, it is not being reviewed properly. D. Sullivan said he believes a positive recommendation would be inappropriate so it would come down to a neutral or negative recommendation. M. Bingham said the timing is not great. He also stated that he does not remember any municipal projects that got held up by Zoning in the past that would make this amendment a necessity. B. Hoch said he cannot support this amendment either as the Town Planner said the language was confusing. D. Sullivan agreed. M. Bingham made a motion to make a negative recommendation to the Select Board for the proposed amendment as submitted. Seconded by S. Smith. Vote: 4-0-1 (1 abstention by P. Dunn for feeling like she did not have enough information to make a recommendation. J. Perry was recused from this vote and discussion.) Regular Business: 2. Consider a recommendation to the Select Board on the laying out and acceptance of the roadway known as Matt’s Way, part of the Brigham Farm III 9-lot subdivision as a public way. Continued from October 13, 2026 J. Perry rejoined the Planning Board. J. Aubin stated this is a request for the acceptance of the roadway of Brigham Farm Phase III. The final paving has been completed and GPI completed an inspection with Mr. Sagar and M. Mariano today. A list of final outstanding items to be addressed was made and Mr. Sagar is aware of the list. M. Mariano, of Oakhill Engineering, was present to represent Sagar Services for Matt’s Way Road acceptance. He stated that the Board has the completed as-built of the road. The final paving happened last week. There have also been 2 notices of closeout performed. He also captured all the elevations and structures that have been reflected on the as-built. All the bounds had been installed two weeks ago. M. Mariano and G. Sagar went through the final list of items to be addressed from GPI for the Board. M. Bingham made a positive motion to the Select Board with the recommendations stated from GPI and the Town Planner in his report. Seconded by P. Dunn. Vote: 6-0-0 Work Session: 3. Discussion of SNEP Storm water utility technical assistance grant award J. Aubin stated that SNEP is an environmental collaborative of a number of nonprofit agencies and educational facilities that work on environmental technical assistance throughout Southeastern New England. J. Aubin said the Board has worked with them before on this project in 2024 to introduce the idea of a stormwater utility. Next stage includes looking at a feasibility study to assess what it would look like in Seekonk. J. Aubin clarified that this is not proposing anything to town meeting. This is really just an analysis to see what the stormwater costs are currently, what they are projected to be in the future, and how to deal with those costs and budgetary pressures associated. This is being driven by 21st century stormwater issues and storms with 19th century infrastructure. Also, Seekonk is subject to MS4 permitting through the State and the EPA. This was a subject that was discussed with the quad-board to develop a task force working group to work with SNEP to see what this would look like in Seekonk. It also brings into the conversation Home Owner Associations who are dealing with this right now. J. title:
Notice of Public Hearing relative to determination of the percentages of the local tax levy to be
borne by each class of real and personal property for Fiscal Year 2027
text: RECEIVED By City Clerk at 5:54 pm, 11/5/26 CITY OF WESTFIELD NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Notice is hereby given that Westfield City Council will hold a Public Hearing on Thursday, November 19, 2026 at 6:00 P.M. at the regular City Council meeting to be held at the Municipal Building, 59 Court Street, City Council Chamber. Public Hearing relative to determination of the percentages of the local tax levy to be borne by each class of real and personal property for Fiscal Year 2027, as required by Chapter 40, Section 56, as amended by Chapter 718, Section 2, Acts of 1989. At the hearing the Board of Assessors will provide all information and data relevant to the making of such determination and the fiscal effect of the available alternatives. All interested taxpayers are invited to attend and present oral or written information on their views. Written information may be emailed to k.bruce@cityofwestfield.org or be directed by mail to the City Clerk, 59 Court Street, Westfield MA 01085. If mailed, must reach the Clerk’s Office by 5:00 P.M. the day of the hearing in order to be available to the City Council prior to its determination. Kaitlyn Bruce City Clerk/Clerk of the Council

title: November 10, 2026 Yarmouth Select Board Workshop Meeting Agenda
text: TOWN OF YARMOUTH 1146 ROUTE 28, SOUTH YARMOUTH, MASSACHUSETTS 02664-24451 Telephone (508) 398-2231, ext. 1271, Fax (508) 398-2365 SELECT BOARD Tracy Post, Chair Dorcas McGurrin Mark Forest Joyce Flynn Elizabeth Argo ---TOWN ADMINISTRATOR Robert L. Whritenour, Jr. ASSISTANT TOWN ADMINSTRATOR Amy M. Frigulietti WORKSHOP MEETING Per Massachusetts General Law: All town and school boards, committee, and authorities shall post a notice of every meeting at least 48 hours prior to such meeting, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. Notice shall contain a listing of topics/agenda that the chair reasonably anticipates will be discussed at the meeting. As required by Open Meeting Law and Mass. General Law, we are informing you that this meeting will be video and audio recorded, as well as rebroadcast. Anyone intending to video or audio tape this meeting is required to inform the Chair. Yarmouth Select Board November 10, 2026 ~ 6:00 PM Yarmouth Town Hall Hearing Room 1146 Rt. 28, South Yarmouth, MA 02664 This is to formally advise that, as required by M.G.L. Chapter 30A, §§ 18-25, and pursuant to Chapter 20 of the Acts of 2021, An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures Adopted During the State of Emergency, signed into law on June 16, 2021, and extended to March 31, 2027, the Yarmouth Select Board will hold a public meeting on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. in the Hearing Room, Yarmouth Town Hall, 1146 Route 28, South Yarmouth, MA 02664.
